pos: n. (a soft white stone; rendering Greek alabastron)
etymology: From Greek alabastros, a vessel for ointment, often made without handles. The name came to mean the stone itself.
biblical_def: Alabaster is the soft translucent stone from which ointment flasks were cut. Scripture mentions it only in one scene, told in three Gospels: “there came a woman having an alabaster box of ointment of spikenard very precious; and she brake the box, and poured it on his head” (Mar 14:3). The breaking is the point — a sealed flask could not be partly used, so the gift was necessarily total. Christ's defence of her is absolute: “she hath wrought a good work on me… she hath done what she could” (Mar 14:6,8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines alabaster as a sub-variety of carbonate of lime, of a fine white colour, used for vases and ornaments; and a box or vessel for holding perfumes.
webster_full: ALABASTER, n. A sub-variety of carbonate of lime, of a fine white color, and sometimes transparent; used for vases, statues and other ornaments.
2. A box or vessel for holding odoriferous liquors or ointments; anciently made of alabaster.
scriptures: Mar 14:3

And being in Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, as he sat at meat, there came a woman having an alabaster box of ointment of spikenard very precious; and she brake the box, and poured it on his head.
Mar 14:6
And Jesus said, Let her alone; why trouble ye her? she hath wrought a good work on me.
Mar 14:8
She hath done what she could: she is come aforehand to anoint my body to the burying.
Luk 7:37
And, behold, a woman in the city, which was a sinner, when she knew that Jesus sat at meat in the Pharisee's house, brought an alabaster box of ointment,
corruption_summary: Calculated giving asks what portion is appropriate; the alabaster box could not be opened by halves, which is exactly why the disciples called it waste.
corruption_paragraphs: The objection raised against her is one a modern committee would raise: to what purpose is this waste? for it might have been sold for more than three hundred pence, and have been given to the poor. The arithmetic was correct — a year's wages poured out in a moment — and Christ overruled it. Not because the poor do not matter, but because there are acts of devotion whose whole meaning lies in their being unrepeatable and unrecoverable.

She hath done what she could is one of the gentlest sentences in the Gospels, and it sets the standard low enough for anyone and high enough to hurt. Not what she should, not what others did — what she could. The flask was broken because a sealed alabaster vessel had no other way of being opened, and the gift was therefore all or nothing. Some devotion is only real when it cannot be taken back.
roots_summary: Greek alabastron (G211), an alabaster flask for ointment; the stone's softness made it easy to carve and easy to break.
roots_lines: Greek alabastron (G211) — alabaster box; Matthew 26:7, Mark 14:3, Luke 7:37.
Greek muron (G3464) — ointment, perfume; the contents of the flask.
Greek nardos (G3487) — spikenard; the costly import named in Mark 14:3.
usage: “She brake the box, and poured it on his head” — a gift that could not be given by halves.
“To what purpose is this waste?” — the arithmetic was right and the verdict wrong.
“She hath done what she could” — the standard set low enough for anyone.

pos: n. (a lamp, a light; rendering Hebrew ner, Greek luchnos)
etymology: From Latin candela, from candere, to shine. In the KJV candle usually renders words for an oil lamp rather than a wax taper.
biblical_def: A candle is a small light. Christ's use is about placement rather than brightness: “neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick; and it giveth light unto all that are in the house” (Mat 5:15). Proverbs makes conscience the LORD's own lamp: “The spirit of man is the candle of the LORD, searching all the inward parts of the belly” (Pro 20:27). The woman seeking her lost coin lights one and sweeps (Luk 15:8), and Revelation promises a city needing none: “they need no candle, neither light of the sun; for the Lord God giveth them light” (Rev 22:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a candle as a long, but small cylindrical body of tallow, wax or spermaceti, containing a wick, and used for a portable light.
webster_full: CANDLE, n. A long, but small cylindrical body of tallow, wax or spermaceti, containing a wick composed of linen or cotton threads, twisted loosely; used for a portable light.
scriptures: Mat 5:15
Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick; and it giveth light unto all that are in the house.
The spirit of man is the candle of the LORD, searching all the inward parts of the belly.
Luk 15:8
Either what woman having ten pieces of silver, if she lose one piece, doth not light a candle, and sweep the house, and seek diligently till she find it?
Rev 22:5
And there shall be no night there; and they need no candle, neither light of the sun; for the Lord God giveth them light: and they shall reign for ever and ever.
corruption_summary: Christians debate how brightly to shine while Christ's concern was placement — a candle under a bushel is not dim, it is hidden.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 5:15 makes an assumption the church often argues past: the candle is already lit. Christ does not command His disciples to become light; He says ye are the light of the world and then addresses the only remaining question, which is location. A believer whose faith is real but entirely private has not failed to burn; he has installed himself under a bushel, and the light is wasted on the inside of a basket.

Proverbs 20:27 turns the lamp inward and explains why conscience is so uncomfortable. The spirit of man is the candle of the LORD, searching all the inward parts — God's own light, carried inside a man, illuminating rooms he would rather leave dark. That is a mercy before it is a torment: a lamp that shows the dirt is the first requirement for cleaning the house.
roots_summary: Hebrew ner (H5216), a lamp; Greek luchnos (G3088), a portable oil lamp — distinguished from lampas, a torch, and luchnia, the stand.
roots_lines: Hebrew ner (H5216) — lamp, candle; Proverbs 20:27, 2 Samuel 22:29, thou art my lamp, O LORD.
Greek luchnos (G3088) — lamp; Matthew 5:15, Luke 15:8, Revelation 22:5.
Greek luchnia (G3087) — lampstand, candlestick; the seven churches of Revelation 1:20.
usage: “Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel” — the question is placement.
“The spirit of man is the candle of the LORD” — conscience as God's lamp indoors.
“They need no candle… for the Lord God giveth them light” — the city that outgrows lamps.

pos: n. (a fragrant compound; rendering Hebrew qetoreth and raqach)
etymology: From Latin per fumum, through smoke — the earliest perfumes were burned, and the fragrance rose with the smoke.
biblical_def: Perfume is compounded fragrance, and the sanctuary's was legally protected. God gave Moses an exact formula for the holy incense and then forbade its private reproduction: “ye shall not make to yourselves according to the composition thereof… whosoever shall make like unto that, to smell thereto, shall even be cut off from his people” (Exo 30:37–38). Proverbs uses perfume for the pleasure of true friendship: “Ointment and perfume rejoice the heart: so doth the sweetness of a man's friend by hearty counsel” (Pro 27:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines perfume as a substance that emits a scent or odor which affects agreeably the organs of smell; and the scent, odor, or volatile particles emitted.
webster_full: PERFUME, n. A substance that emits a scent or odor which affects agreeably the organs of smell, as musk, civet, or aromatic plants.
2. The scent, odor, or volatile particles emitted from sweet smelling substances.
scriptures: And as for the perfume which thou shalt make, ye shall not make to yourselves according to the composition thereof: it shall be unto thee holy for the LORD.
Whosoever shall make like unto that, to smell thereto, shall even be cut off from his people.
Pro 27:9
Ointment and perfume rejoice the heart: so doth the sweetness of a man's friend by hearty counsel.
And thou shalt make it a perfume, a confection after the art of the apothecary, tempered together, pure and holy:
corruption_summary: The instinct to reproduce holy things for private use is exactly what Exodus 30 forbids, and it survives wherever worship is copied as a technique for producing feelings.
corruption_paragraphs: The prohibition in Exodus 30:38 is startling because the offence is so small: whosoever shall make like unto that, to smell thereto, shall be cut off. Not to sell it, not to profane it — merely to enjoy it privately. The holy perfume belonged to God's presence and nowhere else, and taking its formula home turned an instrument of worship into a personal amenity. That is the enduring temptation: to extract the atmosphere of God's presence and reproduce it for the pleasure it gives.

Proverbs 27:9 shows where fragrance is meant to be enjoyed — in friendship. Ointment and perfume rejoice the heart: so doth the sweetness of a man's friend by hearty counsel. The comparison is exact: counsel from a friend is pleasant the way a good scent is pleasant, and just as unmistakable when it is absent. The verse quietly rebukes a Christianity of solitary devotion by ranking honest friendship among life's genuine luxuries.
roots_summary: Hebrew qetoreth (H7004), incense, that which is burned; raqach (H7543), to compound ointment — the apothecary's verb of Exodus 30:35.
roots_lines: Hebrew qetoreth (H7004) — incense, perfume; Exodus 30:35-38, tempered together, pure and holy.
Hebrew raqach (H7543) — to compound, mix as an apothecary; Exodus 30:33, 35.
Hebrew besem (H1314) — spice, sweet odour; the ingredients of the holy anointing oil.
usage: “Ye shall not make to yourselves according to the composition thereof” — the formula was not for private use.
“Whosoever shall make like unto that, to smell thereto” — the offence was mere enjoyment.
“Ointment and perfume rejoice the heart” — friendship ranked among real luxuries.

etymology: From Greek phiale, a broad flat bowl used for pouring libations. The modern picture of a narrow glass tube is wrong; a vial in Scripture is a wide dish that empties at once.
biblical_def: A vial is a shallow bowl. Revelation gives them two contents. The first is prayer: the four beasts and elders fall before the Lamb, “having every one of them harps, and golden vials full of odours, which are the prayers of saints” (Rev 5:8). The second is wrath: “Go your ways, and pour out the vials of the wrath of God upon the earth” (Rev 16:1). The same vessel-shape holds both, and the shape matters — a broad bowl is not poured gradually but tipped and emptied.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a vial as a phial, a small bottle of thin glass, used particularly by apothecaries and druggists.
webster_full: VIAL, n. A phial; a small bottle of thin glass, used particularly by apothecaries and druggists.
VIAL, v.t. To put in a vial.
scriptures: Rev 5:8
And when he had taken the book, the four beasts and four and twenty elders fell down before the Lamb, having every one of them harps, and golden vials full of odours, which are the prayers of saints.
Rev 16:1
And I heard a great voice out of the temple saying to the seven angels, Go your ways, and pour out the vials of the wrath of God upon the earth.
Rev 8:4
And the smoke of the incense, which came with the prayers of the saints, ascended up before God out of the angel's hand.
Let my prayer be set forth before thee as incense; and the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice.
corruption_summary: Prayer is imagined as vanishing on utterance, when Revelation shows it collected and kept in bowls — and judgment is imagined as arbitrary, when it too is stored before it is poured.
corruption_paragraphs: Revelation 5:8 answers a question every discouraged believer asks: where do the prayers go? They are collected. Golden vials full of odours, which are the prayers of saints, are held in heaven before the throne, and Revelation 8:4 shows the smoke of the incense with the prayers ascending up before God out of the angel's hand. Nothing prayed in faith has evaporated. It is in a bowl, kept, and it is not empty.

The parallel with the vials of wrath is deliberate and sobering. Both are stored, both are full, and both are eventually poured out completely rather than dispensed by degrees. Judgment delayed is not judgment cancelled; it is judgment accumulating in a bowl. That is the same doctrine Paul states as treasuring up wrath against the day of wrath (Rom 2:5), and it should make a patient God look more serious rather than less.
roots_summary: Greek phiale (G5357), a broad shallow bowl for libations — the only New Testament vessel that holds both saints' prayers and God's wrath.
roots_lines: Greek phiale (G5357) — bowl, vial; Revelation 5:8, 15:7, 16:1-17.
Greek thumiama (G2368) — incense, odours; Revelation 5:8, identified as the prayers of saints.
Hebrew qetoreth (H7004) — incense; Psalm 141:2, let my prayer be set forth before thee as incense.
usage: “Golden vials full of odours, which are the prayers of saints” — prayer collected and kept.
“Pour out the vials of the wrath of God” — the same shape, tipped and emptied.
“Let my prayer be set forth before thee as incense” — the psalm behind the image.

pos: n. (the fiftieth year of release; rendering Hebrew yobel)
etymology: From Hebrew yobel, a ram's horn — the year is named for the trumpet that announced it. The KJV spells it with one l.
biblical_def: The jubile is the fiftieth year, when Israel's land returned to its families and her slaves went free: “ye shall hallow the fiftieth year, and proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof: it shall be a jubile unto you; and ye shall return every man unto his possession” (Lev 25:10). The economics rest on a stated theology: “The land shall not be sold for ever: for the land is mine; for ye are strangers and sojourners with me” (Lev 25:23). Isaiah 61's acceptable year of the LORD draws on it, and Christ read that passage in Nazareth and said it was fulfilled.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines jubilee as among the Jews, every fiftieth year, being the year following the revolution of seven weeks of years, at which time all the slaves were liberated and all lands reverted to the former owner.
webster_full: JUBILEE, n. Among the Jews, every fiftieth year, being the year following the revolution of seven weeks of years, at which time all the slaves were liberated, and all lands which had been alienated during the whole period reverted to their former owners.
2. A season of great public joy and festivity.
scriptures: And ye shall hallow the fiftieth year, and proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof: it shall be a jubile unto you; and ye shall return every man unto his possession, and ye shall return every man unto his family.
The land shall not be sold for ever: for the land is mine; for ye are strangers and sojourners with me. for
Isa 61:1

The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me; because the LORD hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek; he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound;
Luk 4:21
And he began to say unto them, This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears.
corruption_summary: Jubilee is treated as a quaint agrarian rule or a political slogan, while its actual claim — that no one finally owns land, because God does — is unwelcome in every economy.
corruption_paragraphs: Leviticus 25:23 is the sentence that makes the whole institution intelligible: the land shall not be sold for ever: for the land is mine; for ye are strangers and sojourners with me. Israel's real estate transactions were therefore leases, not sales, priced by the number of harvests remaining until the jubile. Permanent dispossession was structurally impossible, because a family's inheritance could be temporarily lost but never finally alienated. That is not agrarian nostalgia; it is a theology of ownership with an accounting system attached.

Luke 4 is where the trumpet finally sounds. Christ reads Isaiah's proclamation of liberty to the captives and the acceptable year of the LORD, closes the book, and says this day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears. The jubile was always a rehearsal for a release from a deeper debt, and the congregation that heard the announcement tried to throw Him off a cliff — which is roughly how every settled economy receives the news that the land was never theirs.
roots_summary: Hebrew yobel (H3104), ram's horn, and by extension the year its blast announced; the trumpet sounded on the day of atonement to open it.
roots_lines: Hebrew yobel (H3104) — ram's horn, jubile; Leviticus 25:9-13, Numbers 36:4.
Hebrew deror (H1865) — liberty, release; Leviticus 25:10, proclaim liberty throughout all the land.
Greek aphesis (G859) — release, remission; Luke 4:18, to preach deliverance to the captives.
usage: “Proclaim liberty throughout all the land” — the fiftieth year opened by a horn.
“The land is mine; for ye are strangers and sojourners with me” — the theology under the economics.
“This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears” — the trumpet sounded in Nazareth.

pos: n. pl. (appointed sacred assemblies; rendering Hebrew moed)
etymology: From Latin sollemnis, yearly, customary, religious. A solemnity is not a mood but an appointment — a fixed occasion.
biblical_def: Solemnities are Israel's appointed feasts. Isaiah's promise pictures a city whose calendar is secure: “Look upon Zion, the city of our solemnities: thine eyes shall see Jerusalem a quiet habitation, a tabernacle that shall not be taken down” (Isa 33:20). Ezekiel legislates the prince's part in them (Eze 45:17), and Isaiah 1 shows the terrible possibility that God may hate His own appointed days when the hands that keep them are full of blood: “your new moons and your appointed feasts my soul hateth” (Isa 1:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines solemnity as a rite or ceremony annually performed with religious reverence; and religious ceremony, a ritual performance accompanied with reverence.
webster_full: SOLEMNITY, n. A rite or ceremony annually performed with religious reverence.
2. A ceremony adapted to inspire awe, or to be observed with reverence.
scriptures: Look upon Zion, the city of our solemnities: thine eyes shall see Jerusalem a quiet habitation, a tabernacle that shall not be taken down; not one of the stakes thereof shall ever be removed, neither shall any of the cords thereof be broken.
Isa 1:14
Your new moons and your appointed feasts my soul hateth: they are a trouble unto me; I am weary to bear them.

And it shall be the prince's part to give burnt offerings, and meat offerings, and drink offerings, in the feasts, and in the new moons, and in the sabbaths, in all solemnities of the house of Israel: he shall prepare the sin offering, and the meat offering, and the burnt offering, and the peace offerings, to make reconciliation for the house of Israel.
Isa 1:16
Wash you, make you clean; put away the evil of your doings from before mine eyes; cease to do evil;
corruption_summary: Two errors: treating solemnity as gloom, and assuming that keeping the appointed days guarantees acceptance — which Isaiah 1 flatly denies.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 1:14 is one of the most alarming verses in the prophets because the feasts God rejects are the ones God appointed. Your new moons and your appointed feasts my soul hateth: they are a trouble unto me; I am weary to bear them. The problem was not liturgical error; the ceremonies were correct. The problem is named two verses later — your hands are full of blood — and the remedy prescribed is wash you, make you clean, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow.

Isaiah 33:20 supplies the comfort on the other side. Zion is called the city of our solemnities, and the promise is stability: a quiet habitation, a tabernacle that shall not be taken down; not one of the stakes thereof shall ever be removed. Appointed worship is not a burden imposed on a restless people but the fixed rhythm of a settled one, and its permanence is part of the blessing.
roots_summary: Hebrew moed (H4150), an appointed time or meeting — the same word in tabernacle of the congregation, literally tent of meeting.
roots_lines: Hebrew moed (H4150) — appointed time, feast, assembly; Leviticus 23:2, these are my feasts.
Hebrew chag (H2282) — festival, pilgrim feast; the three annual journeys to Jerusalem.
Hebrew miqra (H4744) — a called assembly, convocation; Leviticus 23:4, holy convocations.
usage: “Zion, the city of our solemnities” — a calendar that cannot be taken down.
“Your appointed feasts my soul hateth” — correct ceremony, bloody hands.
“Wash you, make you clean” — the remedy Isaiah prescribes instead.

etymology: From pure, Latin purus, clean, unmixed. Pureness is a state, not an achievement — what a thing is when nothing foreign has been added.
biblical_def: Pureness is the condition of being unmixed. Paul lists it first among the credentials of a true minister under pressure: “in much patience, in afflictions, in necessities, in distresses… by pureness, by knowledge, by longsuffering, by kindness” (2Co 6:4–6). Proverbs makes it a qualification for high friendship: “He that loveth pureness of heart, for the grace of his lips the king shall be his friend” (Pro 22:11). Job protests his own with the King's knowledge in view (Job 22:30 in context of the innocent), and the beatitude promises sight to the pure in heart (Mat 5:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pureness as clearness, freedom from foulness or dirt; freedom from moral turpitude or guilt; and freedom from improper words or phrases.
webster_full: PURENESS, n. Clearness; freedom from foulness or dirt; as the pureness of water.
2. Freedom from moral turpitude or guilt.
3. Freedom from vicious or improper words, phrases or modes of speech.
scriptures: By pureness, by knowledge, by longsuffering, by kindness, by the Holy Ghost, by love unfeigned,
He that loveth pureness of heart, for the grace of his lips the king shall be his friend.
Mat 5:8
Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God.
Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity.
corruption_summary: Purity is discussed almost exclusively as a sexual category for the young, while Scripture applies it to motives, speech, doctrine, and the handling of money.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 Corinthians 6 lists pureness among a minister's credentials, and the surrounding context is not sexual at all — it is stripes, imprisonments, tumults, watchings, fastings. Paul is describing integrity under pressure: unmixed motives when the ministry is costly and nobody is watching. That is a far broader test than the one the church usually administers, and a far harder one, because sexual purity can be maintained by circumstance while purity of motive cannot.

Proverbs 22:11 draws an unexpected line from the inner life to public usefulness: he that loveth pureness of heart, for the grace of his lips the king shall be his friend. The man is not promoted for ambition or skill but because a clean heart eventually produces gracious speech, and gracious speech makes a man worth having near power. Character is a long strategy, and it is the only one that does not require managing.
roots_summary: Greek hagnotes (G54), purity; hagnos (G53), pure, chaste; Hebrew tohar (H2892), cleanness, from the ritual vocabulary of the sanctuary.
roots_lines: Greek hagnotes (G54) — pureness; 2 Corinthians 6:6 and 11:3.
Greek katharos (G2513) — clean, pure; Matthew 5:8, blessed are the pure in heart.
Hebrew tohar (H2892) — purity, cleanness; Proverbs 22:11, he that loveth pureness of heart.
usage: “By pureness, by knowledge, by longsuffering” — integrity listed among credentials.
“He that loveth pureness of heart… the king shall be his friend” — character as long strategy.
“Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God” — the promised sight.

pos: v. (to set apart to God; rendering Hebrew chanak and qadash)
etymology: From Latin dedicare, to proclaim or devote. To dedicate is to transfer ownership publicly — a declaration as much as an intention.
biblical_def: To dedicate is to set a thing apart for God's use. David dedicates the spoils of war (2Sa 8:11), Solomon dedicates the temple, and the law makes provision for a man who has “built a new house, and hath not dedicated it” to go home from the army until he has (Deu 20:5). Hebrews applies the vocabulary to the covenant itself: “whereupon neither the first testament was dedicated without blood” (Heb 9:18). What is dedicated is no longer available for ordinary use.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines dedicate as to set apart and consecrate to a divine Being, or to a sacred purpose; to devote to a sacred use by a solemn act.
webster_full: DEDICATE, v.t. To set apart and consecrate to a divine Being, or to a sacred purpose; to devote to a sacred use, by a solemn act, or by religious ceremonies.
2. To appropriate solemnly to any person or purpose; to give wholly or chiefly to.
scriptures: Deu 20:5

And the officers shall speak unto the people, saying, What man is there that hath built a new house, and hath not dedicated it? let him go and return to his house, lest he die in the battle, and another man dedicate it.
Which also king David did dedicate unto the LORD, with the silver and gold that he had dedicated of all nations which he subdued;
Heb 9:18
Whereupon neither the first testament was dedicated without blood.
Rom 12:1
I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service.
corruption_summary: Dedication has become a private intention renewed at conferences, where Scripture treats it as a public transfer of ownership that changes what a thing may be used for.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 20:5 reveals how seriously the practice was taken: a man with an undedicated house was excused from battle, lest he die and another man dedicate it. God would rather have the army one soldier short than have a house pass to a stranger unconsecrated. Dedication was not sentiment; it was a legal and liturgical act that determined a building's status, and it ranked above military necessity.

Romans 12:1 carries the vocabulary into the New Covenant with one significant change: the offering is alive. I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service. A dedicated animal could not walk off the altar; a living sacrifice can, which is why Paul grounds the appeal in mercies received rather than in obligation imposed.
roots_summary: Hebrew chanak (H2596), to dedicate or train up — the same verb as train up a child in Proverbs 22:6; qadash (H6942), to make holy.
roots_lines: Hebrew chanak (H2596) — to dedicate, initiate; Deuteronomy 20:5, 1 Kings 8:63, and Proverbs 22:6, train up a child.
Hebrew qadash (H6942) — to consecrate, sanctify; 2 Samuel 8:11 of David's dedicated spoils.
Greek egkainizo (G1457) — to inaugurate, dedicate; Hebrews 9:18 and 10:20, a new and living way.
usage: “Built a new house, and hath not dedicated it” — excused from war until he had.
“Neither the first testament was dedicated without blood” — consecration costs.
“Present your bodies a living sacrifice” — the offering that can walk away.
